items.question: How are the knowledges related to the threefold means arranged in order?
premises: The knowledge connected with the means of the three powers is being described.
The last knowledge is the root.
The others rise in sequence as higher, middle, higher, highest, and first.
items.inference: The knowledges corresponding to the threefold means form an ascending hierarchy grounded in a root knowledge.
uncertainties: The exact mapping of each graded term to a specific means is compressed in the compound.
items.plain_english: Thus the knowledge connected with the means of the three powers is arranged in order: the last is the root, and above it come the middle, higher, still higher, and first levels.

items.question: What knowledge lies beyond the graded knowledges of the means?
premises: There is a knowledge even beyond the previously described levels.
This knowledge is free from means and similar supports.
It rests in the power of bliss and is called unsurpassed.
items.inference: Beyond all method-based knowledges stands a supreme, unsurpassed knowledge grounded in the power of bliss.
uncertainties: The force of ādi in upāyādi could include more than means alone.
items.plain_english: Even beyond that is a supreme knowledge, free from means and the like, resting in the power of bliss; here it is called the unsurpassed.

items.question: How rare and exalted is the unsurpassed self-luminous insight according to scripture?
premises: The insight in question is self-luminous.
Even Vidya and the lords of knowledge find its true attainment rare.
The revered Siddha Tantra states this.
items.inference: Scripture presents this self-luminous insight as supremely rare, beyond even exalted knowers.
uncertainties: The scope of ādi after vidyāvidyeśvara is not specified.
items.plain_english: That self-luminous insight, whose true attainment is rare even for Vidya, the lords of knowledge, and others, is declared in the revered Siddha Tantra.

items.question: Where is this rare insight indicated and under what condition is it revealed?
premises: This insight is indicated in the Malini, in the eighteenth chapter.
It is stated clearly there.
The statement says it is not revealed by Shankara when he is not gracious.
items.inference: The Malini scripture both points to this insight and makes its revelation dependent on Shankara's grace.
uncertainties: The exact nuance of aprasannena could range from unpleased to not graciously inclined.
items.plain_english: This is indicated in the Malini, clearly in the eighteenth chapter, by the statement that it is not revealed by Shankara when he is not gracious.

items.question: What is Abhinavagupta systematizing in the Tantraloka on the basis of this scriptural teaching?
premises: The Malinivijayottara presents a fourfold knowledge.
This fourfold knowledge brings the great rise of attainment and liberation.
Abhinavagupta states that he systematizes it in the Tantraloka.
items.inference: The Tantraloka is presented as a systematic exposition of the Malinivijayottara's fourfold knowledge leading to attainment and liberation.
uncertainties: The precise boundaries of the fourfold knowledge are assumed from context rather than spelled out here.
items.plain_english: On the basis of this very teaching in the Malinivijayottara, I systematize here in this work called the Tantraloka that fourfold knowledge which brings the great rise of attainment and liberation.

items.question: How does any object first appear in reflective awareness, whether inner or outer?
premises: Anything reflectively grasped may be inner or outer.
Such a thing first appears with its form not yet unfolded.
This initial appearance is described as shining forth.
items.inference: All reflective cognition begins with an initial, not-yet-unfolded appearance of its object.
uncertainties: The degree to which parimṛśyate implies deliberate reflection versus implicit awareness is interpretive.
items.plain_english: Here, whatever is reflectively grasped, whether within or without, first shines forth with its form not yet unfolded.

items.question: Under what condition does doubt arise from an initial, not-yet-unfolded manifestation?
premises: An initial manifestation appears with an unfolded form not yet present and an indescribable nature.
Doubt arises only when some form has become determined.
Without such determination, doubt does not arise.
items.inference: Doubt depends on a partial determination within an initially indistinct manifestation.
uncertainties: The relation between nirvācya and the later emergence of determination is compressed.
items.plain_english: Thus the first manifestation, with its form not yet unfolded and its nature still indescribable, becomes doubt only when some particular form has been determined, and not otherwise.

items.question: What is the structure of doubt expressed in the question 'what is this'?
premises: The question 'what is this?' marks the presence of doubt.
In that doubt, some main aspect of the object is already well determined.
Other properties, such as whether it is or is not so, remain not unfolded.
items.inference: Doubt is a mixed state in which one aspect is fixed while other qualifying properties remain unresolved.
uncertainties: The exact referent of mukhya aṃśa depends on the example context.
items.plain_english: In the doubt expressed as 'what is this?', some main aspect of the thing is already well determined, while properties such as whether it is this or not remain not yet unfolded.

items.question: What does the word 'what' actually convey in a state of doubt?
premises: The word 'what' does not add a further meaning beyond the situation.
It points to a thing whose form is not yet opened or articulated.
Thus it denotes the object itself in that unresolved state.
items.inference: In doubt, the interrogative 'what' functions as a bare pointer to an as-yet-unarticulated object.
uncertainties: Whether abhidadhāti is meant in a strict technical sense of denotation is not explicit.
items.plain_english: The word 'what' does not convey any extra meaning; it simply points to the thing itself while its form remains unopened.

items.question: Why is the alternative 'post or person' not the primary form of doubt?
premises: The example 'is it a post or a person?' presents an explicit alternative.
In such a case, many properties are already present and determinations are arising.
Therefore this is not the primary, initial form of doubt.
items.inference: Explicit alternatives belong to a later stage of cognition, not to the primary emergence of doubt.
uncertainties: The compound niścayotpāda could be read as a process or as repeated acts of determination.
items.plain_english: The doubt 'is it a post or a person?' is not the primary kind of doubt, because in that case many properties are already present and determinations are already arising.

items.question: How does renewed doubt differ from explicit conceptual construction?
premises: Doubt can arise again when two possible forms to be reflected on remain not unfolded.
This renewed doubt still belongs to the 'what is it?' aspect.
Explicit conceptual construction is different and clearly distinct.
items.inference: Even renewed doubt remains pre-alternative in structure, unlike the clear conceptual construction of alternatives.
uncertainties: The exact sense of dvairūpya as two forms or two-sidedness is slightly compressed.
items.plain_english: When two possible forms that could be reflected on remain not unfolded, doubt arises again in the 'what is it?' mode; explicit conceptual construction is something else and is clearly different.

items.question: How are the initial statement, the question, and doubt related at the first stage of cognition?
premises: The first stage is the manifestation of a being whose nature is not yet unfolded.
This first stage is called uddeśa here.
It is also identified with question and with doubt.
items.inference: At the earliest cognitive stage, initial statement, questioning, and doubt are aspects of the same not-yet-unfolded manifestation.
uncertainties: The technical force of uddeśa is being introduced and may carry more logical nuance than 'initial statement'.
items.plain_english: Therefore, the first manifestation of something whose nature is not yet unfolded is here called the initial statement; it is also the question and indeed the same as doubt.

items.question: How does self-awareness take on the role of the questioning disciple?
premises: Self-awareness expands along the path of a being whose form is not yet unfolded.
In that expansion it becomes the questioner.
As questioner, it assumes the state of being a disciple.
items.inference: The disciple's questioning role is an expression of self-awareness in its not-yet-unfolded expansion.
uncertainties: The verse states an identity of roles without detailing the mechanism of transition.
items.plain_english: As one's own awareness expands along the path of what is not yet unfolded, it becomes the questioner and takes on the role of the disciple.

items.question: What happens to awareness when inner reflective determination is concealed?
premises: Inner reflective determination can become concealed.
After expansion, withdrawal arises in close succession.
Awareness participates in that rising withdrawal.
items.inference: When inner certainty is concealed, awareness shifts from expansion into a phase marked by withdrawal.
uncertainties: The subject is carried over from the previous verse and is not repeated explicitly.
items.plain_english: When inner reflective determination is concealed, awareness, right after its expansion, also takes part in the rise of withdrawal.

items.question: To what extent is awareness called the questioner in outward expansion?
premises: Outward expansion may become clearly manifest.
Within that expansion, some form may still remain unopened.
Awareness is called the questioner only to the extent that such unopened form remains.
items.inference: The questioning role persists only as long as outward manifestation still contains an unopened aspect.
uncertainties: The balance between prasphuṭa and anunmīlita is relational rather than quantified.
items.plain_english: Even when outward expansion becomes clearly manifest, awareness is called the questioner only to the extent that some aspect of its form still remains unopened.

items.question: What is the ultimate status of the teacher-disciple distinction in question and answer?
premises: Awakening itself takes the form of question and answer.
This same process appears in the roles of teacher and disciple.
The bodily difference between them is not ultimate.
items.inference: The dialogical roles of teacher and disciple are functional expressions within one awakening process, not ultimately grounded in bodily difference.
uncertainties: The verse denies ultimacy to bodily difference but does not deny its practical appearance.
items.plain_english: In this way, awakening itself takes the form of question and answer; so even in the roles of teacher and disciple, the difference of bodies is not ultimately real.

items.question: How does awareness manifest inner multiplicity outwardly as both general and particular?
premises: Awareness, by its very nature as awareness, contains many forms within itself.
It makes these forms appear outwardly.
The example given is a grape appearing through generality and particularity.
items.inference: Outer cognition of general and particular forms is the outward shining of multiplicity already held within awareness.
uncertainties: The example is brief, so the intended scope of sāmānya and viśeṣa is illustrative rather than exhaustive.
items.plain_english: For awareness, being of the nature of awareness, holds many forms within itself and makes them appear outwardly, as in the case of a grape seen through both its general and particular features.

items.question: What kind of manifestation corresponds to the stage of doubt before particulars are fixed?
premises: Some property may be fit for the expectation of a particular aspect that is about to be manifested.
At that stage, what appears is a general manifestation.
This general manifestation is of the nature of doubt.
items.inference: Doubt corresponds to the manifestation of generality prior to the fixing of particular features.
uncertainties: The term sṛṣṭi is used phenomenologically and may not imply literal creation.
items.plain_english: When some property is ready for a particular feature to be manifested but that feature has not yet appeared, what arises is a general manifestation, and that is of the nature of doubt.

items.question: What brings about determination, and why can it not be forced otherwise?
premises: A particular aspect may be about to manifest.
Determination occurs when that particular aspect settles.
This settling follows the inclination of the knowing subject and not mere passage of time.
items.inference: Determination depends on the subject's oriented settling of a particular, not on time alone.
uncertainties: Mātṛruci may imply interest, readiness, or cognitive orientation; the verse leaves it broad.
items.plain_english: When the particular aspect that is about to manifest settles, determination arises; it arises according to the inclination of the knowing subject, and not otherwise, not even after countless ages.

items.question: How do definition, answer, and determination arise from the unfolding of the object?
premises: The object can unfold through mastery of its own power.
This unfolding is a single cognitive act.
By that act arise definition, answer, and determinations.
items.inference: The later logical stages of inquiry emerge from the same act by which the object unfolds itself in awareness.
uncertainties: The compound lakṣaṇottaranirṇayāḥ compresses several stages whose distinctions are developed elsewhere.
items.plain_english: Then, through the object's own capacity to unfold its power, that unfolding occurs; by that same act arise definition, answer, and determination.

items.question: Why does inquiry continue even after some aspect has been determined?
premises: An already determined aspect can be pushed into the background.
Inquiry then proceeds again and again.
This repeated process takes the form of initial statement, definition, and examination.
items.inference: Cognitive inquiry is iterative: each determination becomes the background for further questioning and examination.
uncertainties: The exact technical scope of parīkṣaṇa here anticipates later verses.
items.plain_english: Once a certain aspect has been determined and set in the background, inquiry proceeds again and again through initial statement, definition, and examination.

items.question: In which means of knowing does the triad of initial statement, definition, and examination appear?
premises: Living beings use perception, inference, comparison, trustworthy speech, and other means of knowing.
The triad of initial statement, definition, and examination can appear in all these.
This appearance is presented as universal.
items.inference: The threefold cognitive process operates across all ordinary means of knowing.
uncertainties: The ādi suggests additional pramāṇas without naming them.
items.plain_english: In perception, inference, comparison, trustworthy speech, and other means of knowing, the triad of initial statement, definition, and examination flashes forth for living beings everywhere.

items.question: How do the three stages of inquiry relate to non-conceptual and conceptual cognition, even in perception?
premises: The initial statement is non-conceptual.
Definition is conceptual construction.
Examination is a further series of conceptual constructions, even in direct perception.
items.inference: Inquiry begins non-conceptually but unfolds through conceptual definition and an extended series of conceptual examinations.
uncertainties: The verse compresses how non-conceptual perception and conceptual examination interrelate.
items.plain_english: The initial statement is non-conceptual, definition is conceptual construction, and examination is a further series of conceptual constructions, even in direct perception.

items.question: How do initial statement, definition, and examination appear in the inference about fire on a mountain?
premises: The statement 'this is a mountain' functions as the initial statement.
The statement 'because of smoke it has fire' functions as the definition or inferential mark.
The network of insight into pervasion and related factors functions as examination.
items.inference: The inferential example illustrates the full triad: initial presentation, defining reason, and reflective examination.
uncertainties: The verse uses lakṣyaṃ where the technical stage is lakṣaṇa, which may be a compressed expression.
items.plain_english: In the inference, 'this is a mountain' is the initial statement, 'because there is smoke it has fire' is the defining reason, and the whole network of understanding pervasion and related factors is the examination.
